title: LOT’S DAUGHTERS GOT THEIR FATHER DRUNK TWO NIGHTS IN A ROW—AND BOTH BECAME PREGNANT. BUT THE MOST SHOCKING PART IS WHAT GOD DID GENERATIONS LATER.
paragraphs: LOT’S DAUGHTERS GOT THEIR FATHER DRUNK TWO NIGHTS IN A ROW—AND BOTH BECAME PREGNANT. BUT THE MOST SHOCKING PART IS WHAT GOD DID GENERATIONS LATER.

Genesis 19:30–36 | Two nights of deception. Two pregnancies born from a devastating family tragedy. Two nations with a troubled history. And one astonishing bloodline that would eventually lead to Jesus Christ. This is not a story that excuses sin. It is a story that reveals how far the redeeming grace of God can reach.
There are stories in the Bible that make you want to close the book.
Not because you don't believe God.
But because you cannot understand why something so disturbing would be recorded in His holy Word.
This is one of those stories.
A father. Two daughters. A cave. Wine. Two consecutive nights.
And two pregnancies that should never have happened.
But before you judge this family, before you turn away from the ugliness of what happened, there is something you need to understand.
God did not put this story in Scripture to make evil look acceptable. He allowed this painful history to be recorded without disguising what human beings are capable of doing.
And what happened generations later?
That is where this story becomes almost impossible to forget.
Because one of the children born from this tragedy would become the ancestor of a woman named Ruth.
And Ruth would become part of the family line of Jesus Christ.
Read that again.
The same family history that began with a deeply shameful act would eventually appear in the genealogy of the Savior.
Not because God approved of what happened.
Not because the wrongdoing suddenly became righteous.
But because human sin, however devastating, cannot overturn God's sovereign purposes.
And perhaps someone reading this needs to hear that before we go any further.
Your past may explain some of your wounds. But in Christ, it does not have to determine the ending of your story.
Lot had already lost almost everything.
He had lived in Sodom, a city so deeply corrupted that divine judgment was coming upon it. In Genesis 19, angels came to rescue him and his family before the city was destroyed.
But even their escape was filled with heartbreak.
Lot's wife looked back and became a pillar of salt.
The home they knew was gone.
The world they had built had collapsed.
Lot and his two daughters eventually settled in a cave in the mountains, afraid to remain in Zoar.
Imagine that silence.
No familiar streets.
No ordinary family meals.
No mother to speak to.
No certainty about tomorrow.
Only a father and his two daughters, carrying the trauma of everything they had witnessed.
But the story is about to become darker.
Genesis 19:31–32 records the older daughter saying to the younger:

"Our father is old, and there is not a man in the earth to come in unto us after the manner of all the earth: Come, let us make our father drink wine, and we will lie with him, that we may preserve seed of our father."
— Genesis 19:31–32, KJV
Those words are chilling.
The older daughter believed there was no available man through whom they could continue their father's family line.
Was she convinced that the destruction had wiped out humanity beyond their immediate surroundings?
Was she speaking from isolation, desperation, or fear that no suitable husband remained?
Scripture does not fully explain her thinking.
And we should not pretend to know what God has not revealed.
What Scripture does reveal is that she proposed an act of sexual wrongdoing against her own father, deliberately using intoxication to prevent his awareness.
This was not a romantic encounter.
This was not an expression of love.
This was a profoundly disordered decision involving incest and the exploitation of a person rendered incapable of meaningful consent.
And the Bible does not invite us to celebrate it.
The first night, the daughters made Lot drink wine.
The older daughter went in and lay with him.
Genesis 19:33 says that Lot did not know when she lay down or when she arose.
The next day, she told her younger sister what had happened and urged her to do the same.
So they made their father drink wine again.
And the younger daughter repeated the act.
Two nights.
Two daughters.
One father who, according to the biblical account, was unaware of the acts as they occurred.
Then Genesis 19:36 delivers its devastating conclusion:
"Thus were both the daughters of Lot with child by their father."
There is no attempt to make the scene beautiful.
No sentimental music.
No noble speech.
No declaration that their desperation justified their actions.
Only the terrible consequences of human decisions in a broken world.
And here is something we must never forget when reading difficult passages of Scripture:
The Bible's description of an event is not automatically God's approval of that event.
Scripture records murder, betrayal, adultery, oppression, sexual violence, and devastating family failures.
Not because God delights in those things.
But because His Word tells the truth about humanity.
The Bible is not a collection of carefully edited stories about people who always made the right decisions.
It is the revelation of a holy God working in a world that desperately needs redemption.
And that distinction matters.
Especially when we come to the question that makes this passage so difficult.
Why would Lot's daughters do something like this?
We know what they said.
They wanted to preserve their father's offspring.
But the text does not give us permission to declare that their actions were morally acceptable because they were afraid.
Fear can explain a person's thinking without justifying their behavior.
Desperation can help us understand a decision without making it righteous.
Trauma can leave people profoundly disoriented without turning wrongdoing into holiness.
And this is where the story begins to touch our lives.
Because most of us have never faced anything remotely like what happened in that cave.
But many of us understand what it means to make a terrible decision while afraid.
You were afraid of being abandoned.
So you compromised.
You were afraid of losing someone.
So you lied.
You were afraid of being alone.
So you stayed where you knew you should not stay.
You were afraid of the future.
So you tried to control what belonged in God's hands.
And afterward, when the panic passed, you were left looking at the consequences.
Perhaps you whispered something you never imagined you would say.
"What have I done?"
There is a difference between understanding why someone sinned and pretending that the sin was harmless.
God calls us to face both truth and mercy.
And there is another uncomfortable detail in this account.
Lot's daughters did not suddenly appear in the biblical story without a history.
Earlier, in Genesis 19:8, Lot had offered his daughters to a violent crowd outside his house.
That was a grievous failure of protection.
The text does not tell us precisely how that earlier event affected their later decisions. We must not invent psychological explanations and present them as Scripture.
But it does show us something disturbing about the moral environment surrounding this family.
Their story included failures of judgment, protection, and responsibility long before the cave.
Sin rarely affects only the person committing it.
Its consequences can move through households.
Its wounds can shape relationships.
Its patterns can influence generations.
Yet Scripture never teaches that children are doomed to repeat the sins of their parents.
Nor does it teach that people who have been harmed are destined to become people who harm others.
By God's grace, destructive patterns can be confronted.
Repentance is possible.
Healing is possible.
A different future is possible.
And now the story takes a turn that many readers never see coming.
The two daughters gave birth.
The older daughter named her son Moab.
The younger named hers Ben-ammi.
Genesis 19:37–38 identifies them as the ancestors of the Moabites and the Ammonites.
These nations would later have complicated, frequently hostile relationships with Israel.
But the name Moab is especially important.
Because centuries later, another woman enters the biblical story.
She is not living in a cave.
She is not planning deception against her father.
She is not repeating the wrongdoing of her ancestors.
She is a widow.
A foreigner.
A woman who has experienced loss.
And she makes a decision that will change the course of her family history.
Her name is Ruth.
And she is a Moabite.
Let that settle into your heart.
Ruth came from the people descended from Moab, the son born to Lot's older daughter.
Yet Ruth's own story is marked by extraordinary loyalty, courage, humility, and faith.
When her mother-in-law Naomi prepared to return to Bethlehem, Ruth refused to abandon her.
She said:
"Thy people shall be my people, and thy God my God."
— Ruth 1:16, KJV
Do you see the contrast?
An earlier generation acted out of fear over preserving a family line.
Generations later, Ruth entrusted her future to the God of Israel.
One story involved deception and exploitation.
The other became a beautiful testimony of covenant loyalty and faithful love.
And the connection between them is not an excuse for the earlier sin.
It is evidence that the sins of one's ancestors do not have to define one's own faithfulness.
Ruth did not choose the circumstances of her ancestry.
But she did make a decision about the God she would follow.
There is a powerful Hebrew word associated with the kind of loyal love celebrated throughout the book of Ruth.
חֶסֶד — ḥesed
It is commonly translated according to context as steadfast love, kindness, loyalty, or covenant faithfulness.
In Ruth 3:10, Boaz speaks of Ruth's kindness using this very word.
And Ruth 2:20 also uses ḥesed in a passage about enduring kindness.
This is not merely a feeling.
It is love demonstrated through faithful action.
Love that refuses to abandon someone simply because life has become difficult.
Love that carries responsibility.
Love that acts with integrity.
Love that reflects something of God's own steadfast faithfulness.
And the woman who embodied such loyalty was a Moabite.
Not a woman with a spotless ancestral record.
Not someone whose family history contained no shame.
A Moabite.
Perhaps you can already see where this is going.
But stay with me.
Because the next name changes everything.
Ruth eventually married Boaz.
Their son was Obed.
Obed became the father of Jesse.
Jesse became the father of David.
And from David's royal line, generations later, came Jesus Christ.
Matthew 1:5–6 explicitly places Ruth in the genealogy leading to David, and Matthew 1:16 brings that genealogy to Jesus, who is called Christ.
The genealogy is not an accidental detail.
It is part of the biblical testimony to God's faithfulness across generations.
And yes, this means that the ancestry of Ruth, the Moabite woman, connects the disturbing events of Genesis 19 to the earthly family history recorded in the genealogy of Jesus.
But we must say this carefully.
God did not need Lot's daughters to sin in order to accomplish redemption.
The Bible never teaches that their wrongdoing was necessary, righteous, or commanded by Him.
Nor does the appearance of Ruth in Christ's genealogy mean that God approved of incest.
It means that God was not defeated by a sinful family history.
He brought forth faithful people from a lineage marked by brokenness.
And through His sovereign grace, a Moabite woman became part of the ancestry of the promised Messiah.
That is a much greater truth than pretending evil was secretly good.
Because evil remains evil.
Sin remains sin.
But God's redemptive power is greater than the history of sin.
Think about the people listed in the genealogy of Jesus.
Matthew does not present an ancestry scrubbed clean of every uncomfortable story.
He mentions Tamar.
He mentions Rahab.
He mentions Ruth.
He refers to the wife of Uriah, recalling the deeply painful history involving David and Bathsheba.
These women have different stories, and their circumstances must not be treated as morally identical.
But together, their inclusion reminds us that God's redemptive history unfolds among real people, with complicated histories, suffering, courage, failure, and faith.
Jesus entered the world through an actual human family line.
He did not come to a world that had already repaired itself.
He came into a world that needed saving.
And this brings us to the center of the Gospel.
The most important part of this story is not that Lot's daughters became pregnant.
It is not even that Ruth descended from Moab.
It is that Jesus Christ came to redeem sinners.
Not to celebrate their wrongdoing.
Not to minimize their victims' suffering.
Not to rename darkness as light.
But to confront sin, bear its judgment for His people, and offer forgiveness and new life through His death and resurrection.
The apostle Paul writes:
— 1 Timothy 1:15, KJV
And in the Greek text, the word translated "save" is:
σῶσαι — sōsai
From the verb sōzō, meaning to save, rescue, or deliver.
Christ came to save sinners.
Not merely to give wounded people an encouraging message.
Not merely to make broken people feel better about their past.
He came to reconcile us to God.
He came to deal with the guilt and power of sin.
He came to bring those who trust Him from condemnation into life.
And salvation is not earned by having a respectable family history.
It is received by grace through faith in Jesus Christ.
Ephesians 2:8–9 makes that unmistakably clear.
This is why the Gospel is such astonishing news.
You cannot rewrite yesterday.
You cannot undo every word you spoke.
You cannot erase the consequences of every choice.
You cannot change the family into which you were born.
But through Christ, your past does not have to be the final authority over your identity or your future.
And if you were the person harmed by someone else's wrongdoing, hear this with particular care.
What someone did to you was not proof that you were worthless.
You are not required to call abuse good.
You are not required to excuse someone who violated your trust.
You are not required to return to an unsafe relationship to demonstrate forgiveness.
Biblical forgiveness does not erase accountability, and reconciliation requires more than words.
The God who calls sinners to repentance also cares about those who have been wounded by sin.
Jesus does not ask you to pretend that evil never happened.
He invites you to bring the truth into His light.
Perhaps that is why this story feels so uncomfortable.
It exposes the things we would rather keep hidden.
The family secrets.
The shame nobody discusses.
The decisions that still hurt.
The generational patterns everyone recognizes but nobody wants to confront.
The moments when fear became stronger than wisdom.
And the terrible temptation to believe that a broken beginning must produce a broken ending.
But Ruth's life stands as a witness against that despair.
Her ancestry did not prevent her from trusting the Lord.
Her nationality did not place her beyond the reach of His mercy.
Her widowhood did not make her life meaningless.
And her faithfulness was not wasted.
She became part of a story far greater than she could have imagined.
What about you?
What if the thing you have been carrying for years is not something you are meant to keep hiding, but something you need to bring honestly before God?
What if the sin you keep defending is the very thing Christ is calling you to confess?
What if the shame you keep rehearsing is the very burden you need to surrender to His mercy?
What if your family's past has been speaking louder in your mind than God's promises?
Listen to the words of 2 Corinthians 5:17:
"Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new."
The Greek expression translated "new creature" is:
καινὴ κτίσις — kainē ktisis
A new creation.
Not a person who has somehow acquired a perfect past.
Not someone who will never face consequences or struggle again.
But someone whose relationship to God has fundamentally changed through union with Christ.
That is the promise.
Not that every scar disappears overnight.
Not that repentance removes every earthly consequence.
Not that faith guarantees a painless life.
But that in Jesus Christ, there is real forgiveness, a new identity, and the transforming work of the Holy Spirit.
That is why we must not reduce grace to a slogan.
Grace is not permission to continue in sin.
Romans 6:1–2 explicitly rejects that idea.
Grace teaches us to renounce ungodliness and live differently, as Titus 2:11–12 explains.
The same Savior who forgives also calls us to follow Him.
The same mercy that welcomes the repentant also transforms the way they live.
And sometimes the first evidence of transformation is a painfully honest confession.
"Lord, I was wrong."
"Lord, I have been hiding."
"Lord, I need Your forgiveness."
"Lord, help me stop repeating what has destroyed my family."
"Jesus, teach me to live differently."
Maybe that is the prayer you need tonight.
Not a polished speech.
Not a performance for people who think you have everything together.
Just the truth.
Because you cannot impress God into loving you.
And you cannot hide a wound from the One who already sees it.
If you are struggling to break an old pattern, you can simply comment, "Pray for me."

And if the Lord has already helped you walk away from something that once controlled your life, consider sharing a brief testimony. Your words may encourage someone who has begun to believe that change is impossible.
Not every testimony needs dramatic details.
Sometimes the most powerful testimony is simply this:
"I was heading in the wrong direction. Jesus showed me mercy. And by His grace, I am learning to walk differently."
There is someone reading that who may desperately need to know they are not alone.
And there may be someone on your Facebook friends list who would never walk into a church, never open a Bible, and never ask a pastor for help.
They might stop at the title.
They might recognize their own family pain.
They might discover that Scripture does not hide the darkness of human life.
And they might, perhaps for the first time, understand why the world needs Jesus.
That is why sharing matters.
Not because every share will change someone's life.
But because God's Word is worth making known.
Because there may come a day when you need to remember that God's grace is not limited by the brokenness of your ancestry.
And if you have been following Gospel Warrior, you know why we continue telling these stories.
We do not want to produce content that merely shocks people.
We want to bring people back to Scripture.
To Jesus Christ.
To repentance and faith.
To truth that does not compromise holiness.
To grace that does not deny accountability.
To discipleship that continues long after the emotional moment has passed.
These resources are intended to help people study Scripture, strengthen their faith, grow in spiritual discernment, and build a more consistent walk with the Lord.
Invite your family.
Invite your friends.
Invite the believer who has grown spiritually tired.
Invite the person who has questions about Christianity.
Even invite the skeptic who is willing to examine what Scripture actually says.
Not everyone will agree with every article.
But everyone deserves an opportunity to encounter the truth of God's Word.
And for those who want to help sustain and expand this work, there is another meaningful way to participate.
For believers who choose to give from a heart of generosity, this can be part of their personal Christian stewardship and offering of support.
But let us be biblically clear.
It does not purchase God's favor.
It does not replace salvation by grace.
And it should not automatically be described as the biblical tithe owed to one's local church.
Scripture teaches us to give willingly, thoughtfully, and cheerfully, not under compulsion.
As 2 Corinthians 9:7 says:
"God loveth a cheerful giver."
If you are already faithfully supporting your local church, caring for your family, or facing financial hardship, please do not feel obligated to take on another commitment.
You can still be part of this mission by praying, reading, commenting, following, and sharing biblical truth.
Those products are not the reason we preach Christ.
That you would know Jesus Christ.
That you would study His Word.
That you would turn from sin and trust His grace.
That you would grow in holiness, humility, and love.
And that the truth of the Gospel would reach beyond your own life into the lives of others.
Because in the end, this article was never really about a cave alone.
It was about the terrible reality of sin.
The consequences of fear-driven decisions.
The wounds that can run through generations.
The remarkable faith of a Moabite woman named Ruth.
And the Savior whose coming fulfilled promises far older than any of them.
Lot's daughters tried to preserve a family line through a deeply sinful act.
Ruth, descended from that line, demonstrated faithfulness to the God of Israel.
And Jesus Christ, born generations later, came not merely to preserve a family name but to save His people from their sins.
Matthew 1:21 says:
"Thou shalt call his name JESUS: for he shall save his people from their sins."
There it is.
The center of everything.
Not the scandal.
Not the cave.
Not the ancestry.
Jesus.
And when Jesus saves, He does not merely give the sinner a better reputation.
He gives the repentant believer forgiveness, reconciliation with God, and new life.
That is why no human scandal should ever become more important to us than the holiness and mercy of the Savior.
So before you leave this article, consider one final question.
Are you allowing your past to have the final word over your life?
Or will you bring your past, your present, your guilt, your grief, and your future before Jesus Christ?
You cannot change the first chapter of your life.
But you can turn to the Savior who makes all things new.
If this message has touched you, comment what you are trusting God to transform in your life, as much or as little as you feel comfortable sharing.
And never forget the truth that stands above every broken family history:
The scandal may be written into your history, but it does not have the authority to write your eternity. Jesus Christ alone is the Savior who can redeem what sin has broken.
